segments.spoken: Fable five point two is here, and the demos are wild! But is it worth the hype and the cost? Let's break it down.
First, look at the use cases. One creator asked for a dot and shared a short animated film, complete with music.
Another showed a timeline of human progress stretching into an imagined future. Those future dates are storytelling, not scientific predictions.
Then a creator asked for a self-portrait and got a moving, code-generated pattern instead of a face. These are creator demonstrations, not a promise that every prompt works first time.

The official changes matter too. Anthropic says output can be up to thirty percent faster than Fable five point one, with improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. Adaptive thinking stays on, and higher effort lets it work harder on demanding tasks.
segments.on_screen_text: Up to 30% faster output · Effort controls

segments.spoken: Now the price: standard A P I rates fell twenty percent, from ten dollars in and fifty dollars out, to eight dollars in and forty dollars out per million tokens. Fast mode costs extra, and a subscription still has usage limits.
segments.on_screen_text: 2 · Standard API pricing · $8 in / $40 out per MTok

segments.spoken: Now the practical part. In the reference, the creator asks for an interactive cyberpunk Tokyo street, then shows neon lighting, moving cameras, and sound.
That is the workflow to learn: specify the scene, the camera, the interactions, and the output, then review what it actually produces.
You can reuse a skill to keep those requirements together, instead of rewriting a giant prompt each time. I've made a starter checklist with a scene prompt, performance checks, and a review step.
It won't guarantee a perfect one-click result, but it gives your next build a clear direction. Follow me and comment FABLE for the starter skill!

segments.spoken: Fable five point two more than doubled GPT-six Astra on this robotics benchmark!
In Anthropic's reported tests, robotics was about sixty-five percent versus thirty.
Remote work tasks: forty-one percent, versus about twenty-one for Opus and GPT-six Astra.
Humanity's Last Exam, with tools: seventy-four versus fifty-seven. Real coding projects: seventy versus Gemini's sixty-one.
Computer use: eighty-nine versus almost eighty. Scientific research tasks: roughly seventy-five versus sixty-five.
Its restricted twin, Mythos, scored seventy-six against GPT-six Cyber's sixty-one on a cybersecurity evaluation. These are specific tests, not proof that one model wins everything.
Against the previous Fable, robotics and remote-work scores more than doubled.
And a team of a thousand agents formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in thirty hours, making the proof machine-checkable. That wasn't a new discovery of the theorem.
Opus reached about a quarter in the same comparison.
You can use Fable five point two in Claude Code if your account has access. Choose it for demanding work, check your costs, and review the result.
